entities.name: Ubaldo of Gallura
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ubaldo II Visconti, also known as Ubaldo of Gallura, emerged as a pivotal figure in the complex political landscape of 13th-century Sardinia, serving as Judge of Gallura from 1225 until his death in 1238. Born into the influential Pisan Visconti family, his reign marked a significant, albeit temporary, peak of Pisan influence on the island, challenging both papal authority and the aspirations of other Sardinian giudicati. His rule was characterized by a relentless pursuit of power and a strategic matrimonial alliance that briefly saw him control vast swathes of Sardinia, positioning him as a central player in the broader Mediterranean power struggles between Pisa, Genoa, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Papacy.

Ubaldo II inherited the Giudicato of Gallura from his father, Lamberto di Eldizio, consolidating Visconti power in northeastern Sardinia. His most audacious move came in 1238, following the death of Barisone III of Logudoro, when he married the young heiress Adelasia of Torres. This union, orchestrated by Pisan interests, briefly united the Giudicati of Gallura and Logudoro under his direct control. Furthermore, Ubaldo exerted influence over the Giudicato of Cagliari and even briefly held sway over the Giudicato of Torres, meaning he controlled every giudicato on the island at one point or another, save Arborea, a feat unmatched by any single ruler of his era. This expansion directly challenged the Papacy's claim of suzerainty over Sardinia, leading to repeated papal interventions and excommunications.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ubaldo of Gallura's reign represents a fleeting, yet significant, period where a single ruler nearly unified Sardinia under Pisan influence, directly challenging papal authority and shaping the island's political trajectory for decades. His actions and subsequent death profoundly impacted the balance of power, leading to increased imperial intervention under Frederick II's son, Enzo.
